interviewQuestions.question: How does CRC detect errors, and why is it stronger than a simple checksum?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd explain the mechanism first: CRC treats the data as a binary polynomial, divides it by a fixed generator polynomial using XOR, and sends the remainder along as the check value. The receiver redoes the same division; a nonzero remainder means an error was detected.

The strength comes from the math: a simple checksum (adding up bytes) can miss errors that happen to cancel out in a sum, like a swapped pair of bytes. CRC's polynomial division is specifically designed to catch all burst errors up to the length of the generator, and nearly all longer ones — which is why Ethernet, Wi-Fi, and disk storage all use CRC rather than a plain checksum.

**Testing:** whether you understand CRC as a specific mathematical technique with real detection guarantees, not just "a fancier checksum."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: How CRC works

interviewQuestions.question: Why does the data link layer usually retransmit on error instead of correcting it in place?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it as a cost trade-off: forward error correction needs extra redundant bits sent with every single frame, whether or not an error ever happens — a constant tax. Detect-and-retransmit (ARQ) only pays a cost when an error actually occurs, which is cheaper on links where errors are rare, like typical wired Ethernet.

The calculus flips when a retransmission round-trip is expensive or impossible — deep-space links, one-way broadcast — which is why those use FEC instead. So it's not that retransmission is universally better; it's the right default when round-trips are cheap and errors are rare.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate the cost trade-off rather than just naming both techniques.
